title: A Year of Biblical Womanhood: How a Liberated Woman Found Herself Sitting on Her Roof, Covering Her Head, and Calling Her Husband 'Master'
author: Rachel Held Evans
target_audience: Christians interested in gender roles and biblical interpretation
Readers exploring faith, culture, and the Bible
Women in evangelical or mainline Christian traditions
General readers interested in memoirs with religious and social themes
primary_purpose: To investigate, through personal experiment and research, what it means to follow 'biblical womanhood' literally for a year, raising critical questions about biblical interpretation, gender, and faith in contemporary Christian life.

structure_format.narrative_style: Personal, humorous, diary-style memoir with journalistic elements
structure_format.organization: Chronological, structured by months, each focusing on a different aspect of 'biblical womanhood' (e.g., modesty, homemaking, submission)
features: Reflection essays and interviews with women from different faith backgrounds
Blend of storytelling, biblical study, and cultural critique

key_concepts_lessons: Literal readings of the Bible can clash with modern practicalities and ethics.
Many supposed 'biblical' roles for women are products of cultural context rather than timeless commands.
Faithfulness may involve wrestling with scripture, embracing mystery, and rejecting simplistic answers.
Community, empathy, and humility are crucial in religious and cultural discourse.
Challenging assumptions about womanhood can lead to deeper understanding of God and tradition.
A sense of humor and willingness to experiment can illuminate rigid traditions.
notable_features: Monthly experiment format—one year of living out various 'biblical' roles
Exploration of diverse Christian interpretations (including Amish, Orthodox Jewish, and Quaker women)
Accessible for both faith-based and secular readers
Combines personal narrative with serious theological questioning and social observation
cultural_historical_context: Published in 2012 amid ongoing debates in American Christianity about gender roles, biblical authority, and the rise of the 'Biblical womanhood' movement in evangelical circles. Part of a broader genre of 'yearlong experiment' memoirs popular in the 2000s and 2010s.
reception_impact: Widely discussed in Christian and mainstream media for its innovative approach and critique of evangelical gender norms
Praised for humor and candid spiritual exploration
Helped spark conversations about the complexities of interpreting the Bible in modern contexts
Some critics (mainly from conservative circles) found the approach irreverent or unhelpful for traditionalist readers
comparable_titles: The Gospel of Ruth by Carolyn Custis James
The Year of Living Biblically by A.J. Jacobs
Searching for Sunday by Rachel Held Evans
